strengths: The paper proposes a simple and intuitive alternative to learned compression tokens: selecting semantic anchor tokens from the input and using their KV representations, augmented with anchor embeddings and bidirectional attention. This is a clear architectural contribution in the context-compression literature.
The empirical comparison covers several relevant baselines, including ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL, and LLMLingua-2, across multiple compression ratios and both in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA splits.
The ablation studies are useful: removing bidirectional attention, removing anchor embeddings, varying token selection, and adding AE objectives all help support the main design choices.
The results are generally consistent: SAC improves average F1/EM over soft-compression baselines, with larger gains at higher compression ratios in several settings.
The paper includes some analysis beyond headline accuracy, including attention visualization, representation-space visualization, and pretraining-time comparison.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow for a top-tier venue. Evaluation is limited to MRQA-style extractive QA with a 1B Llama model; there is no evidence on broader long-context tasks such as summarization, multi-document reasoning, retrieval-augmented generation, dialogue, code, or instruction-following workloads.

The main gains over the strongest baseline EPL are modest at 5x compression, often around 0.7 to 1 EM/F1 on averages, and no variance, confidence intervals, or multi-seed results are reported. This makes it hard to judge statistical robustness.

The paper claims inference acceleration and memory benefits but does not provide end-to-end latency, throughput, KV-cache memory, or compression-cost measurements. Since SAC requires running a bidirectional compressor over the full context, the practical efficiency tradeoff is under-evaluated.

The setting uses 510-token sub-context chunks, which weakens the connection to genuinely long-context compression. It is unclear how the method behaves for much longer contexts, cross-chunk dependencies, or cases where the answer requires information spread across distant chunks.

The novelty is incremental relative to existing token-selection and soft-compression methods. Uniformly selecting tokens, marking them, and allowing broader attention is plausible and effective, but the paper does not fully establish why this constitutes a major conceptual advance over combining token selection with trained KV compression.

Important implementation details are underspecified, especially how bidirectional attention is applied while preserving compatibility with the frozen causal target LLM, how anchor KV positions are handled under RoPE, and whether any information leakage or positional mismatch can occur during compression and decoding.

The reproducibility statement is weak in the manuscript text: it refers to an anonymous source-code link, but the visible PDF only says 'This code can be used...' without an actual link or enough standalone detail to reproduce all experiments.

The analysis sections are suggestive but not conclusive. t-SNE plots and attention maps are qualitative, and claims about representations being easier for the target LLM to understand are not rigorously tested with quantitative diagnostics.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: reducing long-context inference cost while preserving downstream performance for LLMs.
The core idea of using selected context tokens as semantic anchors, augmented with anchor embeddings and bidirectional attention, is simple and plausible.

The experimental section includes comparisons against several relevant compression baselines and reports results across multiple MRQA in-domain and out-of-domain datasets at several compression ratios.
The ablations examine the main proposed components, token-selection choices, and the effect of autoencoding objectives, which helps clarify what drives the reported gains.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method appears to combine known ingredients: token selection, learned marker embeddings, KV-based compression, and bidirectional encoder-style attention. The paper does not convincingly establish that this combination is a major conceptual advance over EPL, 500xCompressor, or token-selection compression methods.

The empirical gains over the strongest baseline are often small, especially at 5x compression: e.g., SAC improves over EPL by less than 1 average F1/EM point in several main settings. This does not support the paper’s stronger claims of consistent or significant superiority.

The evaluation is narrow. All downstream experiments are extractive QA-style MRQA tasks with Llama-3.2-1B. There is no evaluation on summarization, multi-turn dialogue, retrieval-augmented generation, long-document reasoning, larger models, or truly long-context workloads, despite the paper’s broad motivation.

The paper motivates context compression by inference acceleration and memory reduction, but provides no inference latency, throughput, memory, or end-to-end cost measurements. Training time is reported, but this is not enough to validate the practical efficiency claims.

The comparison to hard compression is weak: LLMLingua-2 performs very poorly here, but the paper gives little detail on whether it was tuned appropriately or whether stronger prompt-compression baselines were used fairly.

Several claims are overstated. SAC is described as eliminating autoencoding training and being equipped with compression capability a priori, but it still requires substantial LM pretraining and QA finetuning. The evidence supports a training-objective change, not an inherently compression-capable architecture.

The method details are insufficient for confident reproducibility from the paper alone. Important implementation choices such as the exact attention mask, KV reuse mechanism, chunk concatenation behavior, anchor handling across chunks, and decoding interface are under-specified.
No statistical uncertainty is reported. There are no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, which matters because several headline improvements over EPL are small.

The analysis is mostly qualitative and not very rigorous. Attention visualizations and t-SNE plots are used to support semantic claims, but these are weak evidence and are not tied to quantitative causal tests.

The paper’s presentation has notable issues: formatting problems in tables, awkward phrasing, inconsistent claims about attention patterns, and some imprecise terminology reduce confidence in the care of the work.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: reducing long-context inference cost while preserving downstream utility, and it clearly motivates the mismatch between autoencoding reconstruction objectives and task-oriented compression.

The proposed SAC method is conceptually simple and appealing: using semantically meaningful anchor tokens from the original context, adding anchor embeddings, and enabling bidirectional attention during compression. This is a plausible architectural alternative to learned context-agnostic compression tokens.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably strong within the chosen setting. SAC is compared against relevant baselines including ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL, and LLMLingua-2, under multiple compression ratios on both in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA splits.

The ablations are useful and support the main design choices: bidirectional attention, anchor embeddings, token selection strategy, and removal of the AE objective are each studied, with generally consistent trends.
The paper reports implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware, and an anonymous code release, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation scope is narrow: all downstream experiments are QA on MRQA with Llama-3.2-1B as both encoder and target LLM. It is unclear whether the method transfers to larger models, different target LLM families, summarization, retrieval-augmented generation, multi-turn dialogue, or other long-context tasks.

The practical efficiency claims are under-evidenced. The paper motivates inference acceleration and memory reduction, but reports mainly accuracy and training time; it does not provide end-to-end latency, prefill/decoding cost, KV-cache memory, or throughput comparisons at inference time.

The performance gains over the strongest baseline EPL are sometimes modest, especially at 5x compression, where average improvements are below or around one point in several settings. The paper would benefit from significance estimates or multiple seeds to establish robustness.

The novelty is incremental rather than transformative: SAC combines token selection, special embeddings, KV-based compression, and bidirectional encoder attention, all of which are natural extensions of prior compression/token-selection work. The conceptual contribution is useful but not clearly broad-impact.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, the argument that SAC eliminates the need for autoencoding is supported in this architecture and benchmark suite, but the broader conclusion about AE objectives in context compression is not fully established.

The analysis figures are suggestive but not decisive. Attention visualizations and t-SNE plots are qualitative and do not directly prove that the compressed representations are more semantically faithful or causally responsible for the observed gains.

Presentation has several minor issues, including formatting glitches in tables/text extraction, occasional grammatical errors, and some imprecise statements about compression tokens and inference capabilities. These do not invalidate the work but reduce polish.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem in long-context LLM inference: reducing context cost while preserving downstream performance. The proposed Semantic-Anchor Compression idea is intuitive and relevant.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than transformative. SAC combines ideas already present in token selection, KV-cache soft compression, EPL-style position-aware compression, and bidirectional encoding; the paper should position more carefully what is fundamentally new beyond this combination.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: reducing LLM context cost while preserving downstream performance.
The core idea of using selected in-context anchor tokens, augmented with anchor embeddings and bidirectional encoder attention, is simple and reasonably motivated.
The evaluation includes multiple MRQA in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, several compression ratios, ablations for the main components, and some larger-model results.
The reported results are generally favorable against ICAE, 500xCompressor, and EPL, especially at 15x and 51x compression, suggesting the method may be empirically useful.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. SAC appears to combine existing ideas from token selection, positional-layout compression, KV-cache compression, and bidirectional encoding; the conceptual advance over EPL and related soft-token methods is incremental.

The main empirical gains over the strongest baseline are often modest. At 5x compression the average improvements over EPL are below 1 F1/EM, and larger-model results show mixed per-dataset behavior, making the broad claims of consistent superiority feel overstated.

The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier venue. It lacks variance or significance testing, uses limited task families, and gives only shallow long-context summarization/QA results with very low absolute scores.

The fairness of comparisons is not fully established. Some baselines depend on AE+LM training while SAC removes AE; compute, training objective, implementation quality, and hyperparameter tuning may differ in ways that could explain part of the advantage.

The analysis is speculative. Claims about AE interfering with downstream objectives are based on limited gradient and visualization evidence, and the t-SNE/attention-map interpretations do not strongly establish the proposed mechanism.

Reproducibility is weak: the paper states that data, model, and code are released, but the URL is blank in the manuscript. This is a serious issue given the dependence on retrained baselines and detailed implementation choices.

The writing and presentation contain concerning rough edges, including missing release links, occasional grammatical issues, overclaiming, and some unclear metric choices such as calling MRQA F1 'ROUGE-1 F1'.

The paper does not adequately discuss limitations, failure cases, memory/latency tradeoffs during full inference, or how the method behaves under realistic long-context deployment settings beyond small selected experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: reducing LLM inference cost for long-context use while preserving downstream task performance.

The proposed Semantic-Anchor Compression method is conceptually clean: using selected context tokens as compression anchors, adding anchor embeddings, and enabling bidirectional attention gives a plausible architectural alternative to learned special compression tokens and autoencoding-heavy training.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this subarea, covering multiple MRQA in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, several compression ratios, and comparisons to ICAE, 500xCompressor, Activation Beacon, DAST, EPL, and LLMLingua-2.

Results are consistently favorable. SAC outperforms the strongest soft-compression baseline EPL across most reported QA settings, including 5x, 15x, and 51x compression, and the gains are especially clear at higher compression ratios.

The ablations are useful and directly tied to the proposed design: removing bidirectional attention or anchor embeddings hurts performance, and token selection variants help show that the method is not entirely dependent on one hand-picked anchor strategy.

The paper includes additional evidence on scalability to 3B and 8B models, long-context summarization, long-context QA, training curves, representation visualizations, and FLOPs/latency, which strengthens the overall case beyond a single benchmark table.
weaknesses: The main novelty is moderate. SAC is an appealing combination of known ideas: token selection, position-aware soft compression, LoRA-based compression encoders, and bidirectional attention. The paper's own discussion notes that SAC can be viewed as building on EPL, so the conceptual leap is not very large.

The empirical gains over the strongest baseline are real but sometimes modest, especially at 5x compression and for larger 8B models where some per-dataset F1 results are mixed. This supports acceptance, but not a very high-confidence strong accept.

The evaluation is still centered heavily on extractive QA-style benchmarks from MRQA. The long-context summarization and 24K QA experiments are helpful but comparatively limited, with few baselines and only ROUGE/F1-style automatic metrics.

The claim that autoencoding is generally unnecessary or harmful is somewhat stronger than the evidence. The results show this for the tested architectures and tasks, but the analysis does not fully separate effects of objective choice, training budget, model capacity, and architectural changes.

Efficiency analysis is underdeveloped relative to the paper's motivation. The appendix gives FLOPs and one compression latency comparison, but end-to-end decoding latency, memory usage, cache size, throughput under realistic generation lengths, and tradeoffs versus full-context inference are not comprehensively reported.

Reproducibility is weaker than claimed in the manuscript text as presented: the abstract and reproducibility statement say data/model/code are released, but the actual link appears blank or omitted. Important implementation details such as exact preprocessing, anchor insertion behavior across chunks, and evaluation scripts would need to be available for full verification.
The paper lacks statistical significance testing or confidence intervals, despite many close comparisons and many datasets. This makes it harder to judge robustness of smaller gains.

The writing and formatting contain several issues, including missing spaces, malformed table text, and some overclaiming in the analysis. These do not invalidate the work but reduce clarity and polish.
